source.title: Large language models implicitly learn to straighten neural sentence trajectories to construct a predictive representation of natural language

page_placements.theme: Representations and information observables scale differently from mean loss

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures sentence-trajectory curvature, not the loss-scaling laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, or architecture effects on loss in the claim versions. Its own size and training-data results concern curvature instead.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling work and says larger models have better next-word prediction performance, but it does not report held-out loss values or fit loss-scaling laws. The curvature results below are related findings, not tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures sentence-trajectory curvature in GPT-2-family and other models, not held-out loss, compute-optimal allocation, extrapolation, architecture effects on loss, or downstream performance. It cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate Experiment 2. The models trained on 1M-1B tokens were trained to best validation loss, but no loss values are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that trained autoregressive LMs straighten sentence trajectories from early to middle layers. Larger and more-trained models straighten more. Model-generated text is straighter, and curvature correlates with surprisal. They hypothesise straightening drives better next-word prediction. They do not test loss-scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: No loss-scaling-law fitting, extrapolation, or compute-allocation procedure is applied; the study measures representation curvature.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curvature reduction with training-data size appears to plateau: the 1-billion corpus model shows no further reduction relative to the 100-million model.

fits_no_version.finding: Curvature reduction grows with GPT-2-family model size (82M-1.5B); the authors describe the relationship as logarithmic (Fig 3B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-straightening (a curvature reduction) increases roughly log-linearly with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative curvature reduction increases with training tokens from 1M to 100M and plateaus at 1B, while absolute curvature keeps decreasing (Fig 3D, S7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data size increases representation straightening, with relative reduction saturating near 100M tokens.

record.problems: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss, training compute, loss exponents, extrapolation accuracy, or compute-optimal allocations. The size-sweep outcomes are presented graphically without numerical values in the text. Corpus size is described inconsistently as tokens and words in different passages.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; no rows omitted for the row limit. Other results on curvature across layers, generated versus ground-truth sentences, and curvature-surprisal correlation do not test a listed claim version.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is changed to cites_only: Kaplan et al. is cited as motivation, and no loss scaling is measured. The corpus is described as tokens in figure captions and as words in the main text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run loss fits predict loss on much larger runs.

Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
